title: Moghadam, Monaco's Honorary Consul for Nepal, launches relief appeal following devastating floods - Monaco Life
description: Moghadam, Monaco's Honorary Consul for Nepal, launches relief appeal following devastating floods  Monaco Life
publisher.title: Monaco Life
full_article:
Alexander Moghadam, Monaco’s 90-year-old Honorary Consul for Nepal and a well-known local business owner, has started an urgent online fundraiser to help victims of a massive flood that hit northern Nepal on 26th August.

For more than half a century, Alexander Moghadam has been a familiar figure in the Principality. Over 50 years ago, he opened his Persian carpet gallery on the Boulevard des Moulins – it was inaugurated by Princess Grace. While building the business, he quietly established a reputation for local philanthropy through charity auctions backed by his own collection.

Those commercial ties to Nepalese carpet makers eventually led to his appointment as Monaco’s Honorary Consul to Nepal more than 15 years ago. Over the years, he has combined frequent diplomatic visits with active fundraising. Following the devastating earthquake of 2015, his efforts helped finance essential community facilities. As he once recalled in his office, pointing to a modest rug bought cheaply in an Eastern market: “It was sold and resold at auction multiple times, with the proceeds multiplying each time. Thanks to that, we were able to build facilities for the Nepalese people after the 2015 earthquake – all from a tiny rug.”

Through a combination of public donations and personal contributions, his efforts over the last 15 years have funded the construction of a school and housing for more than 600 people.

Photo Credit: Le Boudoir D’Highlights

Responding to a fresh catastrophe

Now, Moghadam is moving to support the region after the 26th August disaster, during which a severe flash flood and debris flow tore through northern Nepal. Originating from the Bhote Koshi river network roughly 80 kilometres from Kathmandu, the flood devastated districts including Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading, and Gorkha. The sheer force and speed of the water swept away homes, bridges, roads, and vital hydroelectric installations in the narrow mountain valleys, leaving families virtually no time to evacuate.

According to the Nepalese government, international sources, and Reuters reports, the humanitarian toll is immense. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered, over 6,000 people remain missing, and more than 13,000 have been rescued, while thousands of others are displaced without homes or livelihoods. Preliminary assessments by the Nepalese government place direct physical damage at roughly $1.8 billion US dollars, with total recovery needs projected at $4.78 billion US dollars.

How to support the campaign

Alexander Moghadam has now launched a digital solidarity network to channel immediate help to those on the ground.

He is urging residents and businesses in Monaco to contribute to a dedicated fundraising page titled ‘We Stand With Nepal’, hosted on Leetchi. All money raised goes directly to the Nepal Red Cross to supply emergency food, clean water, shelter, and medical support to families affected by the disaster.

Contributions of any size can be made online via the Leetchi Campaign Link , and organisers are encouraging supporters to share the link and QR code across personal and professional networks to amplify the relief effort.

title: Nepal rains: 27 killed in rain-induced disasters, authorities say - The Times of India
description: Nepal rains: 27 killed in rain-induced disasters, authorities say  The Times of India
publisher.title: The Times of India
full_article:
Beginning on September 24, Nepal faced catastrophic rainfall that triggered numerous landslides and floods, resulting in the tragic loss of 27 lives.



You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.



At least 27 people have been killed in Nepal by the rain related calamities since September 24, according to the authorities.The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) reports that eight people have been hurt in landslides and floods caused by severe rainfall, while four individuals are still unaccounted for.According to the administration, since September 24, twenty individuals have died in landslides, four in floods, and three in accidents involving severe rainfall.114 cattle were slaughtered and 1,082 households were impacted by the disasters. Additionally, 31 bridges were damaged by landslides and floods, and 227 homes were totally destroyed while 142 others were partially damaged.Between September 24 and 27, 542 rain-related catastrophe situations were documented, according to the NDRRMA.The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology reports say that over the four days ending September 27, 186 rainfall measurement stations nationwide recorded more than 100 mm of precipitation.At 544.2 mm, Dedhgaun in Nawalparasi (Bardaghat Susta East) had the most rainfall, followed by Panchase in Kaski with 500.2 mm and Atraulitaar in Tanahun with 472 mm.The meteorological experts attributed the severe rains to moisture-laden winds from the Bay of Bengal and a low-pressure region near Uttar Pradesh in northern India.Over 980,000 individuals received flood-warning SMS notifications from the NDRRMA via telecom service providers.According to NDRRMA spokeswoman Shanti Mahat, some 2,000 individuals who were at risk of flooding were moved to safer locations. According to her, a helicopter was used to rescue people, who were stranded by landslides, and floods in isolated areas including Jajarkot, Myagdi, and Baglung.For search, rescue, and relief efforts, security troops from the Nepali Army, Armed Police Force, and Nepal Police were sent in.On September 27, a helicopter rescued 78 individuals, who were in danger in Pauddhar of Annapurna Rural Municipality-5 in Myagdi and transported them to a safe location, according to Mahat. Additionally, four individuals, who were stuck on an island in Jajarkot's Bheri River were flown, according to PTI report.According to local media sources, heavy rains caused landslides in Chame, Manang, on the afternoon of September 27. Flood and landslide debris from Ghatte Khola partially blocked the Marsyangdi River, allowing the two streams to join and form a lake.As the river surged, people in Chame and the surrounding regions evacuated to caves, forests, and other safer places. According to local media accounts, a bridge that had been buried started to resurface by Monday, and the lake's water level had dropped by around a meter.Along the Kaligandaki corridor, the water also caused damage to roads and bridges. Kantipur reported that the swelling river was cutting away portions of the road and causing landslides at many sites. Near Ridi and Rudrabeni, more than 50 meters of road were destroyed, and around 30 meters of road were cut at Dedhgaun.The NDRRMA sent out notifications to local bodies and authorities in the affected districts, requesting that they remove families residing in dangerous regions to safer sites and keep a high degree of surveillance in downstream areas.According to the NDRRMA, starting on September 28, water levels in significant rivers, including as the Narayani and Gandaki, began to progressively drop and the situation was generally returning to normal.The most recent floods and landslides occur, when Nepal is still recuperating from the catastrophic flash floods that occurred close to the border between Nepal and Tibet last month.On August 26, the Bhotekoshi River, which flows south from the Himalayan border area, brought flooding downstream, destroying homes, cars, highways, bridges, and hydropower projects. Over 1,450 people were killed, and about 5,000 are still missing.

title: After the Flood, Can China, Nepal, and India Move From Earth Observation to Regional Preparedness? - The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
description: After the Flood, Can China, Nepal, and India Move From Earth Observation to Regional Preparedness?  The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
publisher.title: The Diplomat – Asia-Pacific Current Affairs Magazine
full_article:
The recent Bhotekoshi-Trishuli flood near the China-Nepal border, described as a “mountain tsunami,” occurred at a time when glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) are already melting rapidly. Extreme events like the catastrophic flood are no longer isolated anomalies but signals of a broader regional climate crisis in the fragile mountain region. Translating Earth observation of the HKH into actionable regional preparedness is therefore an urgent requirement for climate action.

The August 26 flood showed how difficult it is to anticipate some of these risks in advance. Scientific assessments and satellite imagery confirm that a massive rock-ice avalanche collapsed into the Chhochen Khola, triggering a cascading flood of water, mud and debris into the Lhende Khola and further downstream. This disaster was a human tragedy, with more than 1,400 people dead and some 6,000. Fertile Trishuli valley lands were taken away, millions of tonnes of carbon credits were destroyed and economic damages added up to billions of dollars.



Failure zone on Mount Langtang Lirung, source of the August 26, 2026 Bhotekoshi–Trishuli flood. Image from Google Earth.

The impact was not confined to Nepal. The “mountain tsunami” obliterated Gyirong Port, the primary border crossing for both people and trading goods moving from Nepal into China. China has reported over 40 people dead and over 50 missing.

Districts along the India-Nepal border were also put on heightened alert. Indian National Disaster Response Force teams were deployed, and people in lowland areas were requested to move to safer places. And Bihar is currently dealing with a much wider flood situation.

And floods continue to hit the region. As of September 27, at least 56 people had died in monsoon-driven flooding in India, and 14 more perished in Nepal. Several rivers, including the Ganga, Gandak, Koshi, Budhi Gandaki, and Bagmati, are above danger levels at various locations.

Other South Asian countries are experiencing similar extreme climate events – floods and inundation. Pakistan’s disaster agency, the National Disaster Management Authority , has recorded 199 deaths since the rainfall began on June 26 of this year. Nearly 2,000 houses have been damaged. Similarly, in July, more than 1 million people were stranded across seven districts after days of heavy rain in Bangladesh.

The events of 2026 are not an aberration. The flood-risk map in the World Risk Report 2025 places Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India among the highest flood risk countries in the world.

Global flood-risk map showing Bangladesh, Pakistan and India among the four highest-risk countries. Map from the World Risk Report 2025, Bündnis Entwicklung Hilft and IFHV.

It is also worth remembering that these events are happening in a region where per capita greenhouse gas emissions (2.5 for India, 1 for Pakistan, and 0.8 for Bangladesh) are well below the global average of 6.4 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent per person. This raises a wider question of climate inequality, as countries contributing relatively little to global emissions face some of the greatest climate risks.

The effect of these floods – not just those on August 26, but all of them – continues long after the water recedes. As recurring floods damage crops, homes, infrastructure, commerce, and local economies, repeated losses can make it harder for families to recover. This can make farming and other local livelihoods harder to sustain in the long run, forcing the victims to opt for migration in the face of extreme vulnerability. A study conducted by the World Bank estimated that South Asia may see about 40 million internal climate migrants by 2050.

Is it possible to mitigate the damage through information sharing? That’s been a topic of much discussion since the August floods hit Nepal.

What Earth Observations Are Showing Across the Hindu Kush Himalaya

Integrated Earth observations – including visual, thermal, and synthetic aperture radar (SAR) remote sensing – alongside localized field surveys demonstrate widespread cryospheric and geomorphic transformation across the broader HKH. Satellite-based observation and in situ monitoring confirm that Himalayan glaciers are experiencing persistent mass loss averaging around half a meter of ice thickness per year , accompanied by widespread snowline depression and declining snow cover. Generally, river flows are stationary, but some experience a temporary increase of discharge due to glacial ice melt.

According to ICIMOD’s 2026 assessment, glaciers across the HKH region are losing ice at roughly twice the rate seen before 2000. Research in the Everest region shows debris-covered glaciers can experience severe thinning, surface lowering of up to 1.56 m/yr, and flow deceleration. Further, recent research indicates that the human-populated area at the Everest Base Camp has a higher surface warming rate compared to the surrounding unpopulated part of the Khumbu glaciers, a major source of the Koshi River system.

This extensive cryospheric decay destabilizes surrounding slopes, as thawing permafrost and paraglacial moraine degradation increase susceptibility to catastrophic rock–ice avalanches and complex hazard chains. A prime example was the August 26 flood, which began with an ice–rock slope collapse from the northern face of Mount Langtang Lirung into the Chhochen Khola and Lhende Khola. The collapse induced seismic energy equivalent to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake and evolved into a destructive debris flow that rushed downstream across Nepal into China and India.

Bridging the Observation Gap: Connecting Satellites, Sensors, and Communities

Field observations and small-scale studies remain limited in the HKH due to logistical challenges, resource constraints, and field risks. Consequently, monitoring relies heavily on Earth observation and remote sensing, while long-term ground measurements of glacier mass balance, snow, and other cryospheric variables remain sparse. Cloud cover, steep terrain, and limited ground validation further constrain even satellite observations.

One study showed that glacial lakes increased in Nepal (in terms of both numbers and surface area) between 1977 and 2017. However, satellite-based inventories mainly capture such lakes’ extent and change. Gauging lake depth, volume, dam condition, and hydrological behavior often requires field measurements or higher-resolution observations.

Major gaps remain in monitoring remote glaciers, snowfields, glacial lakes, unstable terrain, and headwater rivers. The lack of data limits hazard forecasting, water resource assessments, and long-term mountain planning.

Addressing these gaps will require bringing different forms of observation together. Integrating multi-tiered Earth observations would create a comprehensive framework for monitoring dynamic cryospheric hazards across Nepal and the HKH.

E ven though satellite, SAR, and DEM data cover areas well for tracking glacier loss, tools like UAVs, CORS, and automated weather stations give much better detail at specific sites. These tools help to monitor slope instability, ice movement and hydrometeorological conditions.

Complementing these technical solutions, local community observations contribute crucial real-time contextual validation during sudden disaster events. To bridge these diverse inputs, recent scientific assessments emphasize that unifying these streams requires common geodetic reference frames, standardized data protocols, and centralized open-access platforms – such as Mountain GeoPortal – enabling agencies like Nepal’s Department of Hydrology and Meteorology (DHM) to model cascading hazard chains, issue early warnings, and protect downstream river systems.

Downstream authorities and communities across Nepal and the HKH require actionable, localized, and time-sensitive warnings rather than raw scientific data or static maps.

High-priority actionable information includes automated classifications of hazardous glacial lakes, real-time forecasts of peak flood magnitude, expected water and debris arrival times, and dynamic inundation maps highlighting at-risk settlements, roads, and hydropower facilities.

In transboundary river basins like the Koshi and Gandak, saving lives depends on real-time cross-border hydrometeorological data sharing before flood surges cross international borders. Upstream flow warnings allow downstream operators; such as those at the Gandak Barrage-to manage control gates proactively and cushion flood impacts on plains communities.

Ultimately, this data must feed directly into automated multi-language cell alerts and pre-rehearsed local response plans, so communities have enough time to evacuate when necessary.

From Observations to Regional Preparedness

There are already some efforts to build on. Nepal itself is now strengthening monitoring following the recent disaster, and looking for more real-time information from China on glacier movement and upstream water levels. Some of these systems may provide only a few minutes of warning during a very fast event, but even that can matter if information can reach people quickly.

There are also several existing arrangements between countries across the region for sharing flood forecasts, river data and information on mountain hazards. Some of these have been in place for decades.

Afghanistan and Pakistan cooperate through the Flash Flood Guidance System , including flood forecasting tools and technical training supported by the World Meteorological Organization.

Bangladesh and India share real-time flood data through bilateral arrangements and the Joint Rivers Commission to support flood forecasting and early warnings in Bangladesh.

For Bhutan and India, a joint hydrometeorological and flood-forecasting network , established in 1955, supports flood warnings for rivers flowing from Bhutan into Assam and West Bengal.

India and Nepal carry out joint flood forecasting and river management through established bilateral mechanisms, including for the Koshi and Gandak river systems.

China and India have an Expert Level Mechanism on Trans-border Rivers , which provides a channel for technical discussions. Earlier agreements covered flood-season hydrological data sharing for the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, but both have expired, and regular data sharing remains suspended .

China and Nepal cooperate on disaster prevention, emergency management, and information sharing . Nepal and China also exchange hydrological and meteorological information, including information on flood risks and glacial lakes.

China and Pakistan likewise have technical cooperation on hydrological and geological hazards , including glacier risks, monitoring technologies and early-warning systems.

As for India and Pakistan, the Indus Waters Treaty (1960) provides for hydrological data exchange and flood-related notifications. However, India announced that it was holding the treaty in abeyance in 2025. Pakistan maintains that the treaty remains binding and rejects its unilateral suspension.

These mechanisms show that cooperation is happening, but there are still key gaps. Data sharing between some countries has been interrupted, while other mechanisms focus mainly on routine flood forecasting or technical exchanges. There is also limited coordination on how warnings are passed between institutions and used by authorities downstream, particularly when hazards develop quickly and leave little time to respond.

These issues are also getting more attention at the political level. Around the time of Nepal’s devastating floods, parliamentarians from across the HKH met in Bhutan to discuss regional collaboration. Days later, another round of parliamentary dialogue took place in Thimphu, focusing on finding efficient ways to link scientific evidence with policy, budgets and disaster preparedness.

While these arrangements and platforms already exist, there are still gaps in how monitoring information is shared and used operationally, particularly for hazards that can move rapidly across national borders.

Two priorities seem particularly important here. Monitoring systems need to be designed in a way that communities and authorities downstream can easily use. It should include practical information, like where risks may emerge, who could be affected, and how much time they have to prepare.

There is also scope for countries to do more joint planning around shared risks, building on existing arrangements. This could include assessing possible impacts across borders, agreeing on how warnings reach the relevant authorities, and testing these arrangements together. For some Himalayan hazards, there may be very little time to respond, so much of this work needs to happen in advance.

Other regions already have some systems that could offer useful lessons for the region. For example, the Mekong River Commission has formal procedures for countries to share data on water flows, floods, and other basin conditions. It also runs a regional flood and drought center that combines monitoring data with forecasts and shares them with national agencies and the public. This model cannot be directly applied to the Himalaya where geography, politics and types of hazards are different. But there are useful lessons in how countries can make cross-border data sharing more regular and reliable.

Conclusion

The HKH is experiencing rapid glacier loss, bedrock failures, and growing risks from cascading hazards, affecting communities, infrastructure, and economies.

title: In Nepal’s premium rental market, the dollar is everywhere but on paper - The Kathmandu Post
description: In Nepal’s premium rental market, the dollar is everywhere but on paper  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
When Sachin Dangi arrived in Pokhara for two months of work, the cheapest decent apartment he could find cost him $30 a day. Not 4,600 in Nepali rupees, but 30 US Dollars. He rented it and was the only Nepali living in the building. What Dangi had run into was a rental market that, in practical terms, had stopped catering to people like him. After all, if he decided to stay at the apartment for two months, he would have to pay about Rs276,000.

“The lowest price I could find was $20 to $30—Rs3,000 to Rs4,600 a day,” said Dangi, founder and chief executive officer of Saarang, a web-based platform for tourists. “For a foreigner, that’s still pretty cheap.” At Paramount Apartment, where he stayed, the math made sense to him. “The feeling you get is that this place is not for a Nepali audience,” he said.

What Dangi experienced has, over the past several years, become the default logic of the premium rental market in cities like Pokhara. The issue is even graver in Kathmandu. In neighbourhoods like Sanepa, Jhamsikhel, Baluwatar, Lazimpat, realtors estimate that 40 to 60 percent of listings are now priced in US dollars, a currency that, according to the country’s central bank and lawyers, private landlords are not legally permitted to charge. No regulator has ever tested that law. No government agency currently tracks how widespread the practice has become. The Post spoke to about a dozen officials, lawyers and economists who are responsible for overseeing the arrangement, each of whom said someone else was responsible.

The scale of what has been built is clear. Records from the Department of Urban Development and Building Construction show that Bagmati Province is home to 79 of the 80 multi-unit apartment projects approved nationwide as of the last fiscal year. Out of 6,943 approved housing units, 6,905 are in Bagmati Province. The office does not keep any record of which of those buildings are marketed to foreign tenants, or in what currency their rent is set. Doing so goes beyond the jurisdiction granted to the office, said Prabesh Shrestha, an engineer at the department.

According to Jitendra Gopal Shrestha, director of Cosy Nepal, one of Kathmandu’s earliest apartment rental platforms, there was no apartment concept to speak of twenty years ago. “Nepalis don’t have the culture of hosting guests long-term,” he said. “Most of them have caste-based considerations when renting.”

Sun City Apartment, Kathmandu. Angad Dhakal/TKP

Shrestha said he started his business in 2013 watching two trends intersect—joint families breaking into nuclear ones, and a steady flow of expats into the Valley who needed furnished housing for months at a time.

What he built has since been replicated dozens of times over. But what began as a solution to a genuine housing gap has evolved into something else: an investment vehicle built explicitly to attract foreign tenants—diplomats, INGO staff, researchers and non-resident Nepalis whose remittances flow home in dollars which most Nepali renters do not earn.

Narendra Lohar, a realtor at Charkilla, one of Kathmandu’s more active property agencies, has had a ringside view of the changing market. In the premium areas he covers, including Sanepa, Lazimpat, Jhamsikhel, Thamel and Bhainsepati, the cost of renting a property has seen a steep rise over the years. “Previously, it was just $700 to $800 per month,” he said. “Now it has increased to $900 to $1,100 which is roughly a 30-35 percent increase.”

The pricing logic originates almost entirely with landlords. “The landlords set the price themselves,” Lohar said. “They ask us for suggestions but it’s usually them who come up with the price.” Landlords generally raise rents by about 10 percent each year, in line with standard Nepali rental practices. But when rents are set in foreign currency, the 10 percent increase is applied to the foreign-currency amount rather than the rupee value. The result is a market that inflates in two currencies simultaneously.

LB Thapa, the owner of a newly built 5,500 sq ft residence near Lemon Tree Hotel in Budhanilkantha, said his property—featuring seven bedrooms and six bathrooms—was recently listed exclusively “for foreigners only.” He is targeting embassies for long-term tenancy. His minimum asking rent is $9,860—or Rs1.5million a month and it is negotiable.

Why only foreigners? What if a Nepali tenant agreed to Thapa’s terms and price? Thapa said that most Nepalis cannot afford it but added that if any Nepali agreed to his terms and price, he’d rent it. “But why would a Nepali pay so much money?” he said.

Lohar said that landlords also calculate that dollar mostly appreciates. For many, it is the return calculation that justifies constructing the property at all, he said.

What landlords, realtors and property managers have built is, on paper, a practice that the country’s laws do not permit.

Chapter 9 of Nepal’s Civil Code, 2018, governs residential tenancy. Section 391 states that rent must be paid by cheque or cash in Nepali currency or cheques exchangeable within Nepal. “It does not say ‘such-and-such currency’ or ‘dollars’, but Section 391(3) makes it clear that this refers to Nepali rupees,” said Sakun Bhandari, a property lawyer practising for 13 years.

The living area of a fully furnished Sanepa apartment marketed to premium, often foreign, tenants. Photo: Courtesy of NRES

The Foreign Exchange (Regulation) Act, 2019 adds further weight. Section 4 bars foreign exchange transactions without approval from NRB. “The law contains no explicit prohibition by name, this is where the gray zone enters, but neither does it permit dollar-denominated rent,” Bhandari said. “Within Nepal’s territory, if any landlord rents out their house, land, or apartment, they must use Nepali rupees. Doing it in USD in itself becomes an incorrect practice.”

There is further practical constraint. Rental agreements above Rs20,000 must be certified by the local ward office where the property is located. If such an agreement arrived at a ward office denominated in foreign currency, the office would likely refuse to certify it, Bhandari said. “None of our laws state that rental agreements can be done in foreign currency. That’s where the problem can arise.”

When asked whether any landlord had ever been prosecuted, any tenant had ever filed a challenge, or any court had ever ruled on this practice, the answer was the same across every institution contacted for this story—no. “Such issues have not come up so far,” Bhandari said.

Sudha Shrestha, deputy spokesperson of Nepal Rastra Bank, confirmed that under Section 4 of the Foreign Exchange Act, transactions in foreign currency without NRB permission are not permitted. But she added that NRB itself has no enforcement authority. That authority was recently transferred, per a gazette notification dated July 29, 2026, to the Department of Money Laundering Investigation, or DMLI. Previously it lay with the Department of Revenue Investigation.

An officer at the DMLI told the Post no such case has ever been brought to his department. “The specific nature of this issue you are raising has not been seen here at all,” the officer said, under the condition of anonymity. The officer added that his department was handed the authority for less than two months and it has received no complaint so far.

At the Baluwatar Ward Office, for instance, the picture is equally uncertain. Nabin Mainali, a ward committee member, confirmed that agreements are registered in Nepali rupees and that a USD-denominated agreement presented would likely be refused by the ward.

Guna Raj Bhatta, an economist at NRB, said he had not been aware the practice was active in Kathmandu’s prime location, until the questions were put to him. “Transacting or doing business in dollars is not allowed in Nepal,” he said. “Even if a foreign tourist comes here, they have to transact using Nepali currency. Our law itself has banned foreign currency transactions; there is no doubt about that.”

There was, however, doubt about everything else.

In practice, the dollar is present everywhere except the official record. Listings appear online in dollars. Landlords and agents negotiate in dollars. The conversion to rupees happens at the moment of formal agreement, just before the contract is registered at the ward office, and just often enough to satisfy whatever scrutiny exists. “For foreign clients we just price the list in USD as it is easy for them to understand but in the legal document, it’s in Rs,” said Lohar, the Charkilla realtor. “We negotiate and keep a flexible amount as it should be okay for the owner and also for the client. When paying, they convert USD into Nepali.”

What complicates this further is the payment chain involving landlords who live abroad. A manager at one of Sanepa’s premium apartment complexes described an arrangement that has become common practice. Most landlords whose properties command dollar rents are Nepalis living abroad, in the United States, Dubai, Singapore, who manage the lease paperwork themselves and keep it formally compliant with Nepali law. But the actual transaction bypasses Nepal’s banking system entirely. Tenants transfer rent in US dollars directly to the landlord’s international account, or in many cases, to the account of the landlord’s child studying at a university abroad. The rent, in effect, funds tuition.

Sapkota of DMLI flagged this dimension. “If a cross-border transaction link is found, the laws regarding Hundi can also be attracted,” he said. The channels for moving money across borders—such as Western Union, MoneyGram, informal hawala networks—are used. His department has not yet received a formal complaint on this practice.

Photo: Courtesy of NRES

Shrestha, the director of Cosy Nepal, described a version of this in the context of his own platform: international listings are quoted in dollars, converted to rupees at transaction, and received into Nepali bank accounts. “We don’t have to deal with NRB,” Shrestha said. “Even if card transactions are done, the currency is converted into Nepali. The money comes in Nepali bank.” This is the legal model. But between this and the arrangement where rent disappears into an offshore account accessed by a landlord’s child studying abroad, the distance may be shorter than the paperwork suggests.

The dollar premium is no longer confined to Kathmandu. In Pokhara, the pattern Dangi described has taken hold in a certain way that he called a regulatory gray zone—a rental market where properties register as hotels, list as apartments, operate as short-term rentals, and charge by the dollar.

“There is no legal recognition for hostels and apartments even in Gandaki Province,” Dangi said. Properties advertise as apartments while registered under hotel categories. Safety standards are discretionary—whether to install CCTV cameras, whether to maintain a reception desk, “everything is so wide open to interpretation.” He contrasted this with the hotel sector, which has an association, an inspection process, and a star-rating system. Apartments have none of it.

Lohar confirmed the Pokhara trend and extended it further: in tourist areas including Mustang, properties are priced in dollars as standard. Hotels in Chitwan are now converting rooms into short-term apartment-style rentals, entering a market that operates by the same informal dollar logic with even less oversight. The practice travels with the foreigners, and whenever foreigners go in sufficient numbers, the dollar follows.

Yuxiang, an anthropologist and researcher at a US-based institution conducting fieldwork in Bauddha, was paying approximately $15 per night for accommodation booked through Airbnb. “It’s ridiculously high when we look at local standards,” he said. He had, in a previous visit, rented accommodation in rupees through a mutual friend, negotiated directly and paid in cash. The difference was the channel—Nepali networks price in rupees; international platforms, built for a global audience accustomed to dollar benchmarks, price in dollars. The same city, the same rooms but two different economies.

Shrestha, the Cosy Nepal director who has watched the market evolve for two decades, said he no longer recognises it as the industry he had started.

Since last year, despite the noticeable decline in the number of INGO staff clients, new buildings keep going up. The foreign tenants that premium landlords have built entire buildings to attract are arriving in smaller numbers than before. But the prices continue to rise, and the dollar keeps appearing at the top of every rental listing.

title: After Nepal's deadly floods, displaced families face a long road to recovery - DW.com
description: After Nepal's deadly floods, displaced families face a long road to recovery  DW.com
publisher.title: DW.com
full_article:
One month after deadly flash floods in Nepal swept away Karishma Tamang's community in Rasuwa District, the pregnant 26-year-old is still struggling to find a safe place to call home.

Karishma, who is expecting her second child, has been moving from place to place with her 4-year-old daughter since the devastating floods swept through Nepal's Bhotekoshi-Trishuli river corridor near the Chinese border at the end of August.

"Initially, we were kept in a covered hall at Bidur Municipality in Nuwakot District," she told DW, adding that hundreds of people shared the same shelter for days.

"Now we have shifted to a small makeshift family tent at the nearby Barahachaur area. Still, we can't sleep during rainy nights as it leaks when it rains." Her brother and his two children remain missing after the flood.

Nepal's leaders say the country needs long-term international support to adapt to a rapidly changing mountain environment Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

There is no proper toilet, although a small makeshift latrine has been set up near the tents, Karishma said.

Children and pregnant women like Karishma need privacy and safety, but such facilities remain scarce in the Himalaya nation's flood-hit areas.

"It would be great to have a stable place to stay, where I could cook my own meals, feel safe and have some comfort," she said.

Safety concerns in temporary shelters

The August 26 flood, triggered by a glacier collapse along the Nepal-China border, killed about 1,450 people and left more than 5,500 missing. Reconstruction costs are estimated to be $4.8 billion (€4.2 billion).

At least seven people, including girls, women and local volunteers at temporary shelters and camps, spoke to DW. Although none reported experiencing sexual harassment or abuse, their accounts point to widespread concerns about safety and vulnerability in the aftermath of the floods.

Sabita Tamang, who lost her 5-year-old daughter, nephew and niece in the floods, is also staying in a makeshift tent in Barahachaur. The 24-year-old said she has to travel beyond the nearest tap to bathe and collect water.

Privacy and safety remain scarce in the Himalaya nation's flood-hit areas Image: Niranjan Shrestha/AP Photo/picture alliance

"We feel uncomfortable taking a bath in an open space among strangers and unknown locals," she told DW. "Many children have seen their family members, friends and neighbors caught in the floods," she said, raising concerns about the impact on their mental health and education.

Risk of trafficking and abuse

Save the Children Nepal has warned that protection measures for children and their families must be strengthened across flood-affected areas amid concerns about trafficking, violence, exploitation and child marriage.

Many families have moved into rented rooms. Yet hundreds are being housed in temporary shelters and makeshift tents in Nuwakot and Dhading districts.

Save the Children Nepal raised concerns about privacy and safety for girls and women because unfamiliar people have unrestricted access to shared spaces.

Ayush Joshi, director for advocacy, campaigns, communications and media at Save the Children Nepal, told DW that the organization's report was based on qualitative assessments involving affected people, including women and children, as well as volunteers deployed in flood-hit areas.

The disaster has affected more than 80,000 people. Thousands who lost everything are living in emergency shelters Image: Pedro Pardo/AFP

"Many temporary shelters are built without planning. Camps on the outskirts of towns have inadequate lighting at night and lack separate washrooms and private spaces," Joshi told DW, noting that there is unrestricted access for unfamiliar people.

"Such situations naturally increase the risk of insecurity, potential harassment and exploitation, especially for young girls and children."

According to Joshi, in the aftermath of the disaster, many people became separated from their families, while some children lost their lives and older siblings had to become caregivers for younger siblings.

"In such circumstances, cases of school dropouts and child marriage could increase," he added, referring to Save the Children's field assessment . "We have seen many children facing mental health issues, like becoming angry, frightened and crying loudly. There is a need for socio-emotional healing."

What does the government say?

The Nepali government has also assessed the risks of trafficking and potential child abuse and has collaborated with organizations such as Save the Children, the police and local authorities to strengthen protection measures at displacement sites.

After Nepal floods, survivors return to ruins of their homes To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Chakra Bahadur Budha, spokesperson at the Ministry of Women, Children, Gender and Sexual Minorities, said the government had increased monitoring and surveillance and was raising awareness about gender-based violence and trafficking.

"We have mobilized and kept all relevant stakeholders on high alert to check at points of entry and exit, so as to protect affected people from being trafficked or abused," he told DW.

Authorities took back at least 78 children from two Buddhist monasteries in Kathmandu and placed them in temporary camps. Budha explained that the monasteries had rescued and supported the children, offering long-term shelter, education and employment, but the government discourages such arrangements outside established procedures.

"We have strictly discouraged religious or charitable organizations from keeping children without following legal procedures," Budha told DW. "Adoption has also been discouraged for now, but children can be placed with close relatives, such as uncles and aunts, for their protection after verification of their relationship."

The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) said at least 541 children have either lost their parents or become separated from their families.

Initial assessments indicate that learning has been disrupted for more than 14,000 children across 62 schools and learning centers in flood-affected areas in Dhading, Nuwakot and Rasuwa districts.

title: Incessant rainfall for four days results in 27 casualties in 542 disaster incidents - risingnepaldaily.com
description: Incessant rainfall for four days results in 27 casualties in 542 disaster incidents  risingnepaldaily.com
publisher.title: risingnepaldaily.com
full_article:
Kathmandu, Sept 29: Twenty-seven people have died in 542 disaster incidents across the country, triggered by the recent heavy rains.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said that four people went missing and eight were injured in the disasters that occurred from September 24 to 27.

The disaster incidents affected 1,082 families and 114 livestock were killed. According to the authority, during this period there were 304 landslide incidents, resulting in 20 deaths, while four people went missing and seven were injured.

In the same way, 87 flood incidents were reported during the period which had resulted in four deaths. In 151 incidents related to heavy rainfall, three people died and one person was injured.

Due to heavy rain, 227 houses are completely damaged while 142 houses have suffered partial damage. Floods and landslides have damaged 31 bridges.

According to NDRRMA, during the four days of rainfall, more than 100 millimeters of rain was recorded at 186 rainfall measurement centers across the country. The highest rainfall was measured in Dedhgaun of Nawalparasi (Bardaghat Susta East) with 544.2 millimeters, and 500.2 millimeters in Panchase of Kaski, and 472 millimeters in Atraulitaar of Tanahun.

Heavy rainfall took place in various parts of the country during this period due to the low-pressure system developed in the Bay of Bengal, the NDRRMA stated.

Disaster warning issued to one million people

To reduce the risk of possible disasters, NDRRMA had intensified disaster early-warning and preparation measures even before the rain started.

During the last monsoon period, NDRRMA's 'situation room' continuously monitored weather and disaster risks, shared information, and coordinated between agencies for 76 hours.

Through telecom service providers, flood warning SMS was sent to over 980,000 citizens. Among them, more than 5,000 were engaged in response activities, and around 9,000 tourists were also informed about weather and disaster-related risks, according to the NDRRMA's report.

During that time, the Authority had increased the flood forecast period for major rivers from three days to five days, and for flash floods in small rivers and streams from 24 hours to 48 hours.

Around 2,000 people rescued

NDRRMA spokesperson Shanti Mahat informed that around two thousand people at risk due to annual floods were relocated to safe places. According to her, people trapped in floods and landslides in remote districts like Jajarkot, Myagdi, and Baglung were rescued by helicopter. Security personnel including the Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, and the Nepali Army were deployed for search, rescue, and relief efforts.

"Seventy-eight people at risk in Annapurna Rural Municipality-5, Pauddhar in Myagdi were rescued by helicopter and transferred to a safe place on September 27," she said. The report also mentions that four people stranded on an island in the Bheri River in Jajarkot were airlifted.

Alert issued after rivers dammed by landslides in Manang and Mustang

According to spokesperson Mahat, heavy rainfall caused landslides on the evening of September 27 in Chame, Manang, which disrupted the flow of the Marsyangdi River. Similarly, landslides blocked the flow of the Kaligandaki River in Thasang Rural Municipality-3 of Mustang.

In view of the possible risk, the NDRRMA had sent a notice to the officials of the concerned districts and local bodies to adopt high alert in the lower riverbank areas of both rivers and to evacuate families living in risky areas to safe places.

NDRRMA stated that the water level in major rivers across the country, including Narayani, has been gradually decreasing and the situation is moving towards normal since September 28. (RSS)

title: Iglesia Ni Cristo Extends Humanitarian Assistance to Nepal Following Devastating Floods - Yahoo Finance
description: Iglesia Ni Cristo Extends Humanitarian Assistance to Nepal Following Devastating Floods  Yahoo Finance

full_article:
KATHMANDU, Nepal, September 29, 2026--(BUSINESS WIRE)--The Iglesia Ni Cristo (Church of Christ), under the leadership of Executive Minister Brother Eduardo V. Manalo, has extended humanitarian assistance to Nepal following the devastating floods that caused widespread loss of life and extensive destruction across affected communities.

Through the Felix Y. Manalo Foundation, the humanitarian arm of the Iglesia Ni Cristo, a dedicated Church delegation traveled to Nepal to personally convey the Church's solidarity with the Nepalese people and extend financial assistance for ongoing disaster response and recovery efforts.

The Iglesia Ni Cristo and the Felix Y. Manalo Foundation provided US$200,000, equivalent to approximately NPR 30.556 million, which was formally turned over in Kathmandu to Finance Minister Dr. Swarnim Wagle for the Prime Minister's Disaster Relief Fund.

The assistance comes as Nepal continues to confront the devastating consequences of severe flooding, including loss of lives, missing persons, displacement, and extensive damage to homes, infrastructure, roads, bridges, agricultural lands, schools, hospitals, and hydropower facilities.

The scale of the destruction has been described as unprecedented. Accounts shared in connection with the disaster response characterized the flood as resembling a tsunami, with floodwaters moving with extraordinary speed through areas where communities depended on rivers and surrounding lands for their homes and livelihoods.

Beyond the immediate human toll, the disaster has inflicted severe economic and physical damage. Thousands of homes were reportedly swept away, while critical infrastructure and agricultural areas suffered extensive destruction. The resulting reconstruction and recovery requirements are expected to be substantial.

Speaking during the assistance turnover, representatives of the Nepalese government expressed appreciation for the Iglesia Ni Cristo's contribution and its gesture of solidarity with the people of Nepal.

The assistance was welcomed as an expression of common humanity, particularly as Nepal undertakes rescue, relief, rehabilitation, and reconstruction efforts.

Government representatives also thanked Brother Eduardo V. Manalo for considering Nepal's urgent needs and directing humanitarian assistance to the country, despite the Philippines facing its own disasters and humanitarian challenges.

Meanwhile, former Union Minister and BJP veteran Murli Manohar Joshi has also drawn attention to the allegedly “ill conceived” infrastructure projects in the Himalayas.

Joshi said various construction projects are collapsing due to natural calamities, and roads and other infrastructure were facing severe damage.

“Even in this situation, some governments are disregarding reports from scientists, geologists, earth scientists and experts in agriculture and biodiversity, and are implementing various travel programmes, tourism initiatives and ill-conceived development plans in the Himalayan region, which are rapidly depleting the Himalayas' extraordinary capacity,” he said.

Joshi, who has been critical of the Char Dham highway development project, highlighted that all states in the Himalayan foothills must consider formulating an integrated, holistic development plan for the entire Himalayan region.

title: Nepal dispatch: Bhotekoshi disaster tests the limits of climate adaptation - Jurist.org
description: Nepal dispatch: Bhotekoshi disaster tests the limits of climate adaptation  Jurist.org
publisher.title: Jurist.org
full_article:
Voimo Tamang is a third-year law student at National Law College and a JURIST correspondent based in Kathmandu, Nepal.

On September 24, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah addressed the 81st United Nations General Assembly to bring the country’s devastating Bhotekoshi–Trishuli floods to the centre of the international climate debate. Describing the disaster as a warning for the world, Shah argued that climate catastrophe is not only a humanitarian crisis but a development emergency, as disasters can destroy roads, bridges, schools, homes, farms, and energy infrastructure, forcing vulnerable countries to borrow in order to rebuild. He called for adequate grant-based support, faster and simpler access to climate finance, and stronger international cooperation on climate resilience.

Shah also proposed a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism involving Nepal, India, and China. The proposed mechanism would facilitate the sharing of satellite data and technical expertise, monitoring of dangerous glacial lakes, stronger early-warning systems, and coordinated cross-border assistance during disasters. His proposal reflects a basic reality of Himalayan climate risks: hazards do not stop at national borders.

The August 26 disaster that prompted the speech began when a massive rock-and-ice avalanche near the Nepal–China border developed into a debris flood and swept downstream through the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli corridors. According to the Nepal government’s initial flood briefing , the disaster caused extensive loss of life and damage to homes, roads, bridges, hydropower facilities, and other critical infrastructure. Rasuwa, Nuwakot, Dhading and other districts were affected.

By September 25, it was reported that 1,453 bodies had been recovered, while 4,718 people remained missing. Police also reported that DNA samples were being collected to identify recovered bodies and that thousands of personnel had been deployed for search, rescue, relief, and related operations. Search and identification operations are continuing, and the figures remain subject to change.

The government’s Rapid Damage and Needs Assessment (RDNA) estimated approximately NPR 408 billion in damage and economic losses and approximately NPR 723.31 billion in recovery and reconstruction needs. Infrastructure accounts for the largest share of the reconstruction requirement, including roads, bridges, and energy infrastructure. A more comprehensive Post Disaster Needs Assessment (PDNA) is still underway, which is expected to provide a fuller assessment of the disaster’s economic, social, and other losses.

The scale of the response has also required sustained coordination between Nepal’s disaster-management authorities, security agencies, and local governments. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs’ daily situation updates have documented the continuing search, rescue, and relief operations, in addition to coordinating with neighbouring countries and international partners.

After the disaster, the government introduced a “ one-door ” system to collect and distribute relief. Individuals, private companies, donor agencies, and international organisations have channelled cash and in-kind assistance through designated government mechanisms. The system was intended to prevent irregularities and duplication, and to coordinate distribution through government agencies and local authorities.

The disaster also raises a more difficult question about climate change. A September 2026 assessment by World Weather Attribution (WWA) found that the event began with a catastrophic rock-and-ice avalanche that transitioned into a debris flood. The researchers linked the changing Himalayan environment—including warming, glacier loss, and permafrost degradation—to conditions that can increase the instability of mountain landscapes. The study does not suggest that climate change alone caused the collapse. Rather, it points to climate change as one factor interacting with existing geological vulnerabilities.

This distinction matters. Simply calling the disaster a “climate disaster” risks overlooking its geological causes, while treating it as purely geological ignores evidence that a warming Himalaya is changing the conditions in which mountain hazards occur. The WWA assessment found that the disaster exposed adaptation limits, particularly where existing warning and preparedness systems are confronted with rapidly developing, cascading hazards.

Nepal’s climate policy already recognises the problem of loss and damage. Its 2025 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0) identifies the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD) and the Santiago Network as important sources of support. It also commits Nepal to improving the documentation of economic and non-economic losses and following a “build back resilient” approach to recovery, rehabilitation, and reconstruction.

The Bhotekoshi disaster has now put those commitments to a practical test. Nepal had already been approved for approximately US$20 million under the FRLD’s Barbados Implementation Modalities, based on proposals submitted before the August disaster. Separately, Nepal submitted an urgent request to the FRLD Board on August 31 seeking assistance following the Bhotekoshi disaster. The two forms of funding should not be treated as the same: the first relates to previously submitted proposals, while the second was an emergency request made after the disaster.

This gap between policy commitments and emergency access to finance is where the climate-justice question becomes particularly important. International climate frameworks recognise the vulnerability of developing countries, but communities affected by a disaster cannot rebuild with principles alone. They urgently need funding, technology, and institutional support to prevent a temporary disruption from becoming long-term development loss.

Nepal’s experience also shows why climate justice is not only about compensation. It involves who bears the cost, who has access to decision-making, and whether vulnerable communities can participate in decisions about reconstruction and relocation. The government’s response therefore needs to consider not only how quickly damaged infrastructure can be replaced, but where and how it should be rebuilt.

For a country whose mountain terrain creates unavoidable exposure to geological hazards, resilience cannot mean promising that disasters will never happen. It must mean reducing avoidable vulnerability before the next disaster occurs. That includes stronger early-warning systems, better mountain monitoring, cross-border information sharing, climate-resilient infrastructure, and clearer plans for communities living in high-risk areas.

The Bhotekoshi disaster leaves Nepal with two connected challenges. Internationally, it must turn its call for climate justice into accessible finance and regional cooperation. Domestically, it must ensure that reconstruction does not simply recreate the vulnerabilities that existed before August 26.

The next test will be whether Nepal’s UN appeal translates into concrete climate finance, and whether the government’s reconstruction plans can turn the lessons of Bhotekoshi into stronger protection for communities facing an increasingly unstable Himalayan environment.

publisher.title: WSB-TV
full_article:
CHEROKEE COUNTY, Ga. — A Cherokee County man is holding onto hope, as he waits to hear news about his mother, who is missing after devastating floods in Nepal.

[DOWNLOAD: Free WSB-TV News app for alerts as news breaks]

Mary Sorensen of Canton was on her way home, coming through the immigration center that we’ve seen videos of being wiped away in flood waters.

Sixty-year-old Mary Sorensen was on a trip of a lifetime.

“She was able to hike up to an incredible mountain with incredible views and swim in an incredible lake and experience all these amazing things that she felt would help her get closer to God and experience God’s grace,” explained Sorenson’s son Riley Wildeman.

Sorensen went hiking in China and was on her way home last week when she sent a text to family saying she “thoroughly enjoyed the experience.”

“Then she ended the text with I’m so grateful that you guys are my family,” said Wildeman. “The group that she was with was able to confirm that she (was) in the immigration center at the time that everything happened.”

The video of the catastrophic flooding, triggered by a landslide last Wednesday when a glacier broke off, shows the waters hitting the immigration center at the China- Nepal border, which is Sorensen’s last known location.

Wildeman was teaching when he got the news.

“I just kind of sat in a stairwell and just prayed and cried a bit and thought a bit and prayed some more,” Wildeman said. “We’ve prayed for a miracle the whole time. We’ve prayed a miracle of her being saved, for her to be found.”

TRENDING STORIES:

Newnan teen emerges from woods, attacks high school runner during cross-country meet: Police

Police: Young mother was shot in head, killed inside apartment before body was dismembered

Georgia mother, son found dead after collapsing in yard

Sorensen is one of dozens of people in the Isha Sacred Walks travel group who are missing. The group posted an update on X that said in part, “it’s very unlikely that anyone could’ve survived the force of the flood.”

But Sorensen’s family is hopeful that the grandmother to four girls can make it home.

“There’s a God who will do a miracle that will bring her home,” said Wildeman. “My dad likes to say that if there’s anybody who’s going to come out of this covered in mud and pissed off, it’s probably going to be her.”

Sorensen was set to get back to the US to help her granddaughters with their first few weeks of school. Wildeman says the family has heard from so many people touched by their mom’s story. For the people asking what to do, they say just to pray for Mary. They’re working to get the word out to as many people as possible so they can keep an eye out for her.
